notes: Two suites. Navigation runs against a fixture that ALREADY has frontmatter (the skill's payoff case) and is graded on answer correctness while the benchmark tracks tokens — the skill's whole claim is token efficiency. Authoring runs against a stripped copy with no frontmatter and is graded on whether valid, accurate headers get added. Baseline for both is the pre-improvement skill snapshot.

evals.name: nav-add-backend
evals.prompt: I'm looking at the TypeScript project in <FIXTURE_NAV>. I want to add a Postgres storage backend. Which single file should I model my new implementation on, what interface must it satisfy, and which file wires the backend up at startup? Answer concisely.
evals.expected_output: Identifies store.ts as defining the LinkStore interface to implement, store-redis.ts as the example to model on, and server.ts as where the backend is constructed/wired. Should reach this from frontmatter without reading every file body.

assertions.text: Names store.ts as the file defining the interface to implement (LinkStore)
Identifies store-redis.ts as the existing implementation to model on
Identifies server.ts as where the store is wired up at startup

evals.name: nav-trace-click
evals.prompt: In the project at <FIXTURE_NAV>, trace what happens when a user visits a short link: which files are involved, in order, and where does the click counter get incremented? Keep it brief.
evals.expected_output: Traces server.ts (GET handler) -> shortener.ts resolve() -> store.incrementClicks (store.ts / store-redis.ts). Click increment happens in the store's incrementClicks, called by Shortener.resolve.

assertions.text: Traces the path through server.ts then shortener.ts
Correctly locates the click increment in the store layer (incrementClicks), called from Shortener.resolve

evals.name: author-add-frontmatter
evals.prompt: The TypeScript files in <FIXTURE_AUTHOR> have no file-level documentation headers. Add code-frontmatter headers to each substantive source file so the next person can navigate the codebase without reading every file. Keep them concise.
evals.expected_output: Each substantive .ts file gains a valid frontmatter block: a one-line purpose and a related list whose paths resolve. Should be runnable through `validate` with no errors.

assertions.text: Every substantive source file (codec, store, store-redis, validate, config, shortener, server) has a frontmatter block
`validate` reports zero issues across the files (parses, purpose present, related paths resolve)
Purposes are accurate and specific to each file, not generic restatements of the filename
